title: The Deer of Kasuga
subtitle: When the Sacred Deer Stop Bowing, a Mountain God Has Turned His Face Away

setting.name: Kasuga and the Deer Park of the Floating World
setting.description: Kasuga is an ancient temple-city cradled in a green valley beneath the forested slopes of sacred Mount Mikasa, where wild deer have wandered freely among the people for a thousand years. The deer are no ordinary animals — they are honored as messengers of the kami, the gods of mountain and shrine, and by long custom they have learned to bow their antlered heads to those who feed them. Pilgrims come from across the islands to walk the deer park's mossy lawns, to make offerings at the great vermilion shrine of ten thousand lanterns, and to kneel before the colossal bronze Buddha that sits in eternal serenity within the largest wooden hall ever raised by human hands. But in recent weeks the deer have grown wild and frightened. They no longer bow. They scream in the night and flee from the shrine paths, and the priests whisper that a kami has been wronged — that something sacred was stolen from the mountain, and the god's anger now seeps down into the valley like cold fog.
setting.atmosphere: A place of luminous, fragile beauty laid over a deepening dread. By day, golden light slants through cryptomeria forests and gilds the moss on a thousand stone lanterns; deer drift through the haze like pale ghosts, and the air smells of incense, cut grass, and rain on cedar. But the bells of the shrine ring at odd hours with no hand upon them, the deer bolt at shadows, and after dark the lantern-flames burn an unnatural pale blue. There is a held-breath quality to Kasuga now — the sense of a sacred order coming undone, of politeness stretched thin over panic. Even the most devout pilgrims hurry home before the lanterns are lit. 🦌🏮

keyLocations.name: The Deer Park and the Bowing Lawns
keyLocations.description: A vast open parkland of close-cropped grass, scattered groves, and moss-furred stone lanterns where hundreds of sacred deer roam without fence or keeper. Vendors at the park's edge sell shika-senbei — flat rice crackers made expressly to feed the deer, who have learned over generations to dip their heads in a polite bow to beg for one. It is the spiritual and social heart of Kasuga, normally serene. Now the deer cluster nervously at the park's far edges, refusing to approach the shrine paths, and several bucks have turned aggressive.
features: Stalls selling shika-senbei (deer crackers) tended by the elderly vendor Obaba Yuki, who has fed the deer for sixty years
Hundreds of free-roaming sacred deer, some still gentle, others grown skittish and one great stag with a blood-red scar across its flank
Rows of ancient stone lanterns (ishidoro) draped in moss, some toppled in the deer's recent panic
A worn shrine path of packed earth leading uphill toward the vermilion gate, which the deer now refuse to cross
encounters: Reading the deer's distress — a Wisdom (Animal Handling) check reveals they are fleeing something on the mountain path, not in the park itself
A panicked stag charges anyone who openly carries food near the agitated herd
Obaba Yuki shares the old legend of the deer's first bow and the kami's covenant, if treated with respect
secrets: The blood-red scar on the great stag's flank is not a wound but a brand of corruption — it was the first deer to encounter the angered kami's influence, and it can lead the party to the source if calmed
Obaba Yuki keeps a small fortune of go-en coins (lucky 5-yen pieces) that pilgrims have pressed on her for blessings; she will give one to a courteous party 'for connection'

keyLocations.name: The Hall of the Great Buddha (Daibutsu-den)
keyLocations.description: The largest wooden building in the known world, a vast tiered hall of weathered timber and sweeping tiled roofs whose ridge-beams are crowned with golden horned ornaments. Within sits the Daibutsu — a colossal bronze Buddha, dozens of feet tall, seated in serene meditation with one hand raised in fearlessness. Pilgrims are dwarfed to insects beneath its half-closed bronze eyes. A great pillar near the rear has a hole bored through its base, said to be the size of the Buddha's nostril; those who can squeeze through are blessed. The hall is normally a place of profound calm, but lately the bronze figure seems to weep a thin green verdigris, and monks have found scorch marks on the floor near the altar.
features: The colossal seated bronze Buddha, hand raised in the mudra of fearlessness, eyes half-closed in meditation
Massive cryptomeria-wood pillars, one bored through at its base (the 'Buddha's nostril' — squeezing through grants a blessing, DC 12 Acrobatics for an armored adventurer)
Smoking braziers of incense and offering boxes of weathered wood before the altar
Head Priest Genkō, who tends the hall and first noticed the omens
encounters: Investigating the scorch marks and verdigris 'tears' reveals a yokai entered the hall seeking sanctuary or to defile it
A pilgrim faints before the Buddha, babbling that the statue spoke to them a warning in the old tongue
Priest Genkō explains the proper etiquette of offering and worship — vital instruction for the later ritual
secrets: The 'tears' of verdigris trace the path of the stolen relic — a fleck of its sacred essence was carried through here, and a Religion check reveals the relic was a temple treasure entrusted to the mountain kami
Behind the Buddha's lotus dais is a sealed reliquary niche, now empty, where the stolen object — the Mikasa Mirror — was once enshrined

keyLocations.name: The Shrine of Ten Thousand Lanterns (Kasuga Taisha)
keyLocations.description: A sprawling vermilion-painted shrine complex set into the forested foot of Mount Mikasa, approached through a long avenue of moss-cloaked stone lanterns and hung throughout its eaves with thousands of bronze hanging lanterns green with age. Twice a year the priests light every lantern at once, and the whole shrine becomes a galaxy of flame mirrored in the dark — the Lantern Festival (Mantoro). The shrine is dedicated to the deer-borne kami of the mountain, and its inner sanctum holds the sacred dance-stage where shrine maidens (miko) perform for the gods. The vermilion paint glows like fresh blood at dusk, and the deer that once gathered at its gate now shun it entirely.
features: An avenue of hundreds of moss-covered stone lanterns leading uphill to the vermilion gate (torii)
Thousands of bronze hanging lanterns beneath the shrine's eaves, lit en masse during the Mantoro festival
An open dance-stage where miko (shrine maidens) perform kagura, sacred dances to please the kami
A purification trough (temizuya) at the entrance where worshippers wash hands and mouth before approaching
Kannushi Hideo, the chief priest, and the senior miko Tsubaki, keepers of the shrine's rites
encounters: The Lantern Festival night, when the party must keep the peace as yokai are drawn to the massed flames
Learning the proper ritual of approach (bow twice, clap twice, bow once) and the offering of a go-en coin from Tsubaki
A will-o'-wisp-like onibi (demon-fire) flits among the lanterns, igniting them out of season and luring the unwary toward the forest
secrets: The shrine's oldest lantern, never lit in living memory, will blaze on its own when the angered kami is finally appeased — a sign the party has succeeded
Senior miko Tsubaki has had visions of a 'three-voiced beast' descending the mountain; she is terrified but bound by duty to remain

keyLocations.name: The Five-Storied Pagoda and the Forest Path
keyLocations.description: A slender wooden pagoda of five tapering roofs rises above the treeline at the edge of the shrine grounds, its central pillar (shinbashira) hung like a great pendulum to sway and survive the earth's tremors. From its base, a steep forest path of stone steps and red-lacquered prayer gates climbs into the cryptomeria gloom of Mount Mikasa toward the kami's high places. This is the threshold between the ordered human world below and the wild divine world above. The deer's terror originates somewhere up this path, and pilgrims have stopped climbing it. Mist pools between the trees even at midday.
features: A five-storied wooden pagoda with a swaying central pillar, housing a relic chamber at its base
A forest path of mossy stone steps climbing the sacred mountain, lined with small red prayer gates
Stone fox statues (komainu and inari foxes) marking the boundary of the kami's domain, some recently toppled
Pockets of unnatural cold mist that muffle sound and dim torchlight
encounters: Yokai bandits — masterless ronin turned to thievery — ambush travelers on the lower path
A pack of corrupted shika-spirits (deer driven feral by the kami's wrath) blocks the upper switchbacks
Navigating the mist-shrouded steps without straying off the sacred path (Wisdom Survival)
secrets: One of the toppled fox statues conceals a hollow where a frightened young monk hid the first clue to the relic's theft before fleeing
The pagoda's swaying central pillar hides a climber's route to a high window with a commanding view of the mountain shrine above

keyLocations.name: The Hidden Shrine of the Mikasa Kami
keyLocations.description: High on the shoulder of Mount Mikasa, reached only by the forest path, lies the small and ancient mountain shrine where the kami of Kasuga is closest to the world. It is a humble structure of unpainted cedar weathered silver by centuries, ringed by a sacred rope (shimenawa) hung with white paper streamers, standing in a clearing of impossible stillness. Here the empty reliquary of the Mikasa Mirror should be honored. Here too the source of the corruption festers — for whoever stole the Mirror cracked the kami's covenant with the valley, and the god's grief and rage have curdled into something monstrous that now nests in the sacred grove. The very air thrums with offended divinity.
features: An ancient unpainted cedar shrine ringed by a thick sacred rope (shimenawa) with white paper streamers (shide)
A clearing of unnatural stillness where no bird sings and the deer will not tread
A ritual stone altar where the proper rite of appeasement must be performed (the etiquette challenge)
The corrupted grove beyond, where the angered kami's wrath has given monstrous form to a nue — a chimera-yokai of many beasts
encounters: The Ritual of Appeasement — a multi-step etiquette and offering challenge to calm the kami before violence
The Nue — a corrupted chimera-yokai, the manifestation of the kami's wounded fury, fought only if the ritual fails or the thief must be stopped
Recovering the Mikasa Mirror from where the thief abandoned it when the corruption overwhelmed him
secrets: The thief was no bandit but a desperate man — a former temple guard who took the Mirror believing it would cure his dying daughter; his body lies in the grove, claimed by the corruption he unleashed
The kami is not evil and never was; once the Mirror is restored and the proper rite performed, the god's wrath becomes a blessing, and the deer bow again

synopsis: The adventurers arrive in the sacred temple-city of Kasuga to find its famous sacred deer — long honored as messengers of the gods — grown wild, agitated, and refusing to bow. The priests of the great bronze Buddha and the shrine of ten thousand lanterns believe a mountain kami has been gravely wronged: a sacred treasure, the Mikasa Mirror, has vanished from its reliquary, and the god's anger is bleeding down the mountain as yokai grow bold and the natural order frays. The party must move through the deer park, the colossal Daibutsu hall, and the lantern-shrine gathering clues; keep the peace through a perilous Lantern Festival night; ascend the mist-wrapped forest path past yokai bandits and feral deer-spirits; and finally confront the truth at the kami's hidden mountain shrine — that a grieving father stole the Mirror to save his dying child and was consumed by the corruption he unleashed. There the party must recover the Mirror and either appease the kami through a precise ritual of etiquette and offering, or fight the monstrous nue into which the god's wounded fury has taken shape.
hook: A letter sealed with the deer-crest of Kasuga reaches the party along the pilgrim road, carried by an exhausted young monk named Ren. The chief priest of the lantern-shrine, Kannushi Hideo, writes with grave courtesy: the sacred deer have stopped bowing, yokai stir on the mountain, and a treasure entrusted to the gods has been lost. The priests cannot raise arms within sacred ground, nor can they ascend the mountain where the kami's wrath now dwells. He offers honored lodging, the gratitude of the shrine, and a reward from the temple's coffers to travelers brave and respectful enough to set right what has gone wrong before the Lantern Festival — three nights hence — when the whole valley gathers beneath ten thousand flames and whatever stalks the mountain may come down to feed.

acts.title: Act 1: The Deer That Would Not Bow
acts.description: The party arrives in Kasuga, meets the priests and the deer-keepers, and investigates the unnatural distress spreading through the sacred city. This act emphasizes wonder, etiquette, and investigation, teaching the players the cultural rhythms of the place — how to feed a deer, how to make an offering, how to address a priest — even as dread accumulates beneath the beauty. By its end the party learns that a sacred Mirror has been stolen and the mountain kami is the source of the corruption.
objectives: Arrive in Kasuga and witness the deer's strange agitation in the park
Learn the customs of offering and respect from Obaba Yuki and the priests
Investigate the Daibutsu hall and discover the empty reliquary of the Mikasa Mirror
Speak with Kannushi Hideo at the lantern-shrine and learn of the angered kami
Calm the scarred great stag to gain a guide toward the mountain

scenes.name: Arrival Among the Sacred Deer
scenes.description: The party walks into the deer park at golden hour, when the light is most beautiful and the wrongness most apparent. Deer should be ambling up to beg crackers and bow; instead they cluster at the far treeline, ears flat, and a scarred stag paces the shrine path like a sentinel that has forgotten its purpose. The cracker-vendor Obaba Yuki watches it all with old, frightened eyes.
scenes.readAloud: "The road opens and the valley of Kasuga spreads before you in slants of late-afternoon gold. Moss-furred stone lanterns stand in their hundreds across a sweep of close-cropped lawn, and among them drift the deer — pale, slender, antlered, sacred. 🦌 You have heard the tales: that here the deer bow their heads to beg a cracker, gentle as temple cats. But these deer do not bow. They huddle at the far trees with their ears pinned flat, and one great stag with a livid red scar down its flank paces the uphill path alone, snorting, refusing to let any creature pass toward the vermilion gate beyond. An old woman at a cracker-stall watches you approach, her wrinkled hands twisting her apron. 'Careful, travelers,' she says softly. 'The gods are unhappy. Even the deer can feel it.'"

skillChecks.success: You read the herd's body language clearly: this is not sickness or rut but terror, and its source lies uphill, on the shrine path, not in the park. The deer are fleeing the mountain.
skillChecks.failure: The deer seem simply wild and skittish; you cannot tell what ails them.

skillChecks.success: Obaba Yuki is genuinely frightened, not merely superstitious. She knows something specific and will share it if treated with patience and respect.
skillChecks.failure: You take her for a nervous old woman spreading rumor.

skillChecks.success: You notice that the scarred stag's wound does not bleed and does not heal — its edges shimmer faintly with an oily, unnatural sheen, like a brand rather than an injury.
skillChecks.failure: The stag simply looks like a battle-scarred old buck.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the players' first lesson in etiquette as mechanics. If anyone brandishes food openly near the agitated herd, a panicked deer may charge (a non-lethal hazard — DC 12 Dexterity save or be knocked prone and shoved 5 feet). Obaba Yuki will teach the party how to feed a deer properly: keep crackers hidden, offer one openly with a small bow, and the gentler deer still remember the courtesy. She tells the old legend that the first deer bowed to a god who rode it down from the mountain, and that the deer have bowed ever since 'as long as the gods are honored.' Their refusal to bow now is, to her, the worst omen imaginable. Let the beauty and the dread sit side by side.
loot: A bundle of shika-senbei (deer crackers, 10) — feeding a gentle deer with a bow restores a measure of the herd's calm
A lucky go-en coin (5-yen piece, bored through the center) gifted by Obaba Yuki 'for good connection' if the party is courteous

scenes.name: Beneath the Bronze Buddha
scenes.description: The party visits the colossal Daibutsu hall, the largest wooden building in the world, to pay respects and seek the priests. Beneath the serene half-closed eyes of the great bronze Buddha they find subtle signs of violation — scorch marks, weeping verdigris — and, behind the lotus dais, an empty reliquary niche. Head Priest Genkō receives them and, if shown proper respect, reveals what was taken.
scenes.readAloud: "You pass beneath a gate as tall as a city wall and into a hall of timber so vast that clouds of incense smoke hang in its upper dark like weather. And there it sits: the Daibutsu, a Buddha of bronze the height of ten men, seated in perfect serenity, one great hand raised palm-out in the gesture of fearlessness. Its half-closed eyes seem to regard you with a patience older than the mountains. Pilgrims kneel like grains of rice scattered at its feet. But as you draw near, you see what has troubled the monks: a thin green weeping of verdigris streaks the Buddha's bronze cheeks like tears, and on the polished floor before the altar, dark scorch marks mar the wood — the print of something that should never have crossed this threshold. 🙏"

skillChecks.success: Following the scorch marks and the trail of verdigris 'tears,' you find they lead behind the lotus dais to a small sealed niche — now broken open and empty. Something was enshrined here and is gone.
skillChecks.failure: The marks are disturbing but you cannot make sense of their pattern.

skillChecks.success: You recognize the niche as a reliquary for a treasure entrusted by the temple to the mountain kami — a sacred mirror. Such a theft would shatter the covenant between the valley and its god.
skillChecks.failure: You know the niche held something holy, but its nature and significance escape you.

skillChecks.success: Approaching Priest Genkō with a proper bow and humble words, you earn his confidence. He confirms the Mikasa Mirror was stolen from the reliquary nine nights ago — the same night the deer first refused to bow.
skillChecks.failure: Genkō is courteous but guarded, and will not yet speak openly of the temple's loss.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Reward cultural literacy here. A party that bows on entering, removes muddy boots, lowers their voices, and does not point at or touch the Buddha earns Genkō's immediate trust and faster answers. A party that tromps in armed and loud gets cold formality and must work for every clue. Genkō is gentle, scholarly, and deeply shaken. He explains the basic etiquette of offering — bow, offer, bow — which the party will need later, and notes that the scorch marks suggest a yokai of fire or shadow passed through, perhaps following the stolen Mirror's lingering essence. Have a pilgrim faint dramatically and murmur a warning 'in the old tongue' to plant unease.
loot: Incense sticks blessed at the Daibutsu (3) — burning one steadies the nerves, granting advantage on the next save against fear within the hour
A rubbing of the reliquary's inscription naming the lost treasure: the Mikasa Mirror (quest clue)

scenes.name: The Chief Priest and the Angered Kami
scenes.description: At the vermilion lantern-shrine, the party meets Kannushi Hideo, who summoned them, and the senior shrine maiden Tsubaki. Here the full shape of the crisis is laid bare: a sacred kami of the mountain has been wronged by the Mirror's theft, its grief and rage are corrupting the deer and emboldening yokai, and the Lantern Festival — two nights hence — may draw whatever stalks the mountain down into the crowded valley. The party also learns the proper rite of approach they will need at the mountain shrine.
scenes.readAloud: "The avenue to the shrine climbs between ranks of stone lanterns so old that moss has swallowed their carved faces, and at its top stands a great vermilion gate burning red against the green of the mountain. ⛩️ Beneath eaves hung with a thousand bronze lanterns, a tall priest in white and a young shrine maiden in red and white await you. The priest bows — deeply, the bow of a man asking a great favor. 'I am Hideo, who sent for you. Forgive what I must ask of those who are guests in our valley.' Behind him, the maiden Tsubaki will not quite meet your eyes; her hands tremble around a sprig of sacred green. 'The mountain god is angry,' Hideo says. 'A treasure was taken from the gods, and now the gods take their leave of us. The deer feel it first. Soon the whole valley will feel it.'"

skillChecks.success: You recall the covenant-lore of such valleys: a kami honored with treasure and rite protects the land, but a kami robbed or dishonored withdraws its blessing — and a withdrawn blessing leaves a void that yokai rush to fill. This matches everything you have seen.
skillChecks.failure: The theology is unfamiliar; you grasp the danger but not its underlying logic.

skillChecks.success: You sense Tsubaki is holding something back out of fear. Drawn out gently, she confesses a vision: a 'three-voiced beast' descending the mountain through the mist — a chimera of many animals crying with many throats.
skillChecks.failure: Tsubaki's terror is plain, but she will not say what she has seen.

skillChecks.success: Hideo and Tsubaki teach you the rite of approach to a kami: purify at the water-trough, then at the shrine — bow twice, clap twice, bow once — and present an offering, a lucky go-en coin being most auspicious for restoring a broken connection. You will need this exactly.
skillChecks.failure: You hear the instructions but mistake their order; the ritual will be harder to perform correctly later.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene front-loads the climax's logic: the party will eventually have a choice between a precise ritual of appeasement and a brutal fight, and this is where they learn the ritual's steps. Emphasize that Hideo is asking outsiders to do violence and tread sacred ground precisely because the priests are forbidden to — a source of his shame and gratitude both. Tsubaki's 'three-voiced beast' is the nue, foreshadowed but not named. Let the players ask questions; reward note-taking. If they ask who could have stolen the Mirror, Hideo admits one of the temple guards vanished the same night — a quiet man named Sato whose daughter lay dying of fever. He cannot believe Sato a thief, only a desperate father.
loot: A shrine charm (omamori) blessed by Tsubaki (1 per party member) — a single-use ward granting advantage on one saving throw against a yokai's frightful or charming effect
Written instructions for the rite of appeasement (quest item — purify, bow twice, clap twice, bow once, offer the go-en coin)

scenes.name: Calming the Scarred Stag
scenes.description: To reach the mountain, the party would do well to befriend the scarred great stag that guards the shrine path — the first deer touched by the corruption, and the only one that will willingly approach the mountain again if its fear is soothed. Calming it is a test of patience, courage, and the etiquette of the deer.
scenes.readAloud: "The scarred stag has not left the shrine path in nine days. It stamps and snorts, head low, the oily red brand on its flank catching the dying light. The other deer give it a wide berth, as if it carries something they fear to touch. Yet there is no aggression in its black eyes — only a deep, exhausted dread, the look of a creature that has stood too long between its herd and a darkness it cannot name. If any beast in Kasuga knows the way to the wrong on the mountain, it is this one."

skillChecks.success: Moving slowly, lowering your eyes, and offering a cracker with a proper bow, you reach the trembling stag. It lets you lay a hand on its scarred flank; the brand cools at your touch, and the stag turns its great head toward the mountain path. It will guide you.
skillChecks.failure: The stag bolts, scattering the herd. You may try again, but the agitated deer make a non-lethal stampede hazard (DC 12 Dexterity save or be knocked prone).

skillChecks.success: Examining the brand, you confirm it is no natural wound but a mark of spiritual corruption — proof the source is a kami's wrath, not a disease, and that restoring the Mirror should heal it.
skillChecks.failure: The wound resists your understanding; it neither bleeds nor festers as any wound should.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is a quiet, tender beat before the act break — a chance for a character with a gentle hand to shine. The stag becomes a recurring companion that will lead the party up the mountain path in Act 2 and stand with them at the climax in Act 3, its brand fading as the kami is appeased. If the party never calms it, they can still find the path through Survival checks, but lose a powerful emotional thread and a guide that can sense yokai ambushes one round before they spring. End Act 1 with the stag turning to face the mist-wreathed mountain as the first lanterns of evening are lit — and burning pale, unnatural blue.
loot: The trust of the scarred stag (story companion — senses nearby yokai, granting the party advantage on Perception to avoid ambush on the mountain path)

acts.title: Act 2: The Lantern Festival and the Mountain Path
acts.description: The Lantern Festival night arrives, and the party must keep the peace as ten thousand flames draw yokai down toward the crowded valley. Then, with the festival survived, they ascend the mist-wrapped forest path of Mount Mikasa — past masterless ronin turned bandit and a pack of feral, corrupted deer-spirits — toward the kami's hidden shrine. This act delivers two of the adventure's three honest combats, each with pre-declared DCs and meaningful stakes.
objectives: Keep the peace through the Lantern Festival night as yokai are drawn to the flames
Drive off or extinguish the onibi (demon-fire) luring pilgrims into the forest
Begin the ascent of Mount Mikasa by the forest path
Survive the ambush of the yokai bandits on the lower path
Pass or pacify the pack of corrupted shika-spirits on the upper switchbacks
Find the clue hidden by the frightened young monk and learn the thief's identity

scenes.name: The Night of Ten Thousand Lanterns
scenes.description: On the festival night, the priests light every lantern at the shrine at once, and Kasuga becomes a galaxy of flame. The valley is crowded with pilgrims, the deer huddle in the dark beyond the light, and the party — the only armed defenders permitted near the sacred ground — must watch over the celebration. The corruption draws yokai to the massed fire: pale flames where none were lit, an onibi flitting through the lanterns to lure the unwary into the forest dark.
scenes.readAloud: "At the appointed hour, the priests touch flame to the first lantern, and then — all at once, as if the stars themselves had been called down — ten thousand more catch light. 🏮 The shrine becomes a galaxy. Bronze lanterns blaze beneath every eave, stone lanterns glow along every path, and the whole valley of Kasuga is mirrored in a sea of trembling gold. Pilgrims gasp; children laugh; the miko begin their slow sacred dance upon the stage. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen. And that is precisely when you notice the wrong flames — a handful of lanterns burning not gold but a sick, corpse-pale blue, and among them a single drifting fire the size of a fist, with no lantern to hold it, bobbing toward the dark treeline as a wide-eyed child rises from the crowd to follow it. 💀"

skillChecks.success: You spot the onibi (demon-fire) and the entranced child before either reaches the treeline, with a round to act.
skillChecks.failure: You notice the danger only as the child steps past the last lantern into the dark, costing you precious moments and a clear shot.

skillChecks.success: You recognize the onibi as a corruption-spirit, a will-o'-the-wisp of demon-fire — vulnerable to being doused (a flask of festival sake or the purification trough's holy water disrupts it) or struck while it manifests.
skillChecks.failure: The drifting fire is clearly malevolent, but its nature and weakness are unclear.

skillChecks.success: Joining or steadying the miko's sacred dance, you help hold the crowd's calm and the kami's attention, preventing a panic when the blue flames appear and granting the party advantage on the coming fight.
skillChecks.failure: The crowd senses something amiss; murmurs of fear ripple outward, risking a stampede if the fight goes badly.

enemies: 1 onibi (use will-o'-wisp stats, reflavored as demon-fire)
2 lesser onibi sparks (use will-o'-wisp stats with 9 HP each)
combatEncounters.tactics: The onibi keeps its distance, drifting among the crowd and the lanterns to use bystanders as cover and to lure individuals toward the forest with its Lure ability. It turns invisible (Vanish) after striking and reappears elsewhere among the flames. The party must protect the pilgrims — especially the entranced child — while bringing the fire down. Holy water from the purification trough or blessed incense disrupts its invisibility for one round. If the child is not reached before the onibi crosses the treeline, the child is lured into the dark and must be rescued in the next scene.
combatEncounters.terrain: A crowded festival ground blazing with ten thousand lanterns — bright light everywhere, dense crowds of frightened pilgrims (difficult terrain, risk of trampling), the raised dance-stage, and the purification trough of holy water at the entrance. The treeline is 60 feet from the lit ground; beyond it, darkness.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The tension here is protecting the innocent amid beauty, not just winning a fight. Track the entranced child as a ticking clock — every round the onibi survives, the child takes another step toward the trees. A party that thinks to scoop up the child or splash holy water from the trough should be richly rewarded. If they let the festival devolve into panic, a deer stampede (non-lethal) injures pilgrims and shames the party in the priests' eyes, complicating later aid. Win or lose, the onibi's defeat or escape confirms the corruption is spilling off the mountain and the source must be reached before the next dark.
loot: The grateful family of the rescued child presses a small purse of coin (15 gp) and a jar of pickled plums (umeboshi, 12) on the party
A festival lantern that burns steady gold even in foul air (a light source no wind or yokai-chill can extinguish)

scenes.name: The Bandits on the Lower Path
scenes.description: The morning after the festival, the party begins the ascent of Mount Mikasa by the forest path of mossy stone steps and red prayer gates. The kami's withdrawn protection has emboldened lawless men: a band of masterless ronin, driven to thievery, has staked out the lower switchbacks to rob the few pilgrims still foolish enough to climb. They demand the party's coin and goods — and are not above murder.
scenes.readAloud: "The forest path climbs from the pagoda's foot in steps of moss-slick stone, threading between ranks of small vermilion prayer-gates and the silver trunks of ancient cedars. ⛩️ Mist pools between the trees though the morning is bright, and the deeper you climb the quieter the wood becomes, until even the birds fall silent. At a switchback where two toppled stone foxes flank the path, figures step from the cedar-shadow: half a dozen masterless swordsmen, their robes ragged, their blades far from ragged. Their leader rests a scarred hand on his hilt and smiles without warmth. 'The mountain's no longer safe, travelers,' he says. 'But we can make sure no harm comes to you — for the right price. All of it.'"

skillChecks.success: You convince the bandit leader that this fight will cost him more men than your coin is worth. He pulls back his band — though they will shadow you for a chance at ambush later, removing the element of surprise from the upcoming deer-spirit encounter.
skillChecks.failure: The leader laughs at your bluster; negotiation is over and steel comes out.

skillChecks.success: You read real fear under the bandits' menace — they are starving, frightened men, not killers by trade. A few coins and a warning about what waits higher up may turn some of them aside.
skillChecks.failure: They seem nothing but greedy and dangerous.

skillChecks.success: You appeal to their lost honor as ronin — that there is no glory in robbing pilgrims, and that the true enemy festers above. Two of the band lower their blades and depart, easing the fight.
skillChecks.failure: Talk of honor only hardens the leader's resolve; he takes it as insult.

combatEncounters.tactics: The ronin leader (bandit captain) fights with skill and self-preservation, directing his men to flank from the cedar-shadows and the high ground of the upper switchback. The bandits use the prayer-gates and toppled fox statues as cover and try to isolate the party's softer members. The captain will parley for his life if reduced below half HP and his men are falling, offering information about the 'beast that screams with many voices' he has heard higher on the mountain. If the party reduced their numbers through Persuasion or Intimidation, scale down accordingly.
combatEncounters.terrain: Steep forest switchbacks of mossy stone steps (difficult terrain when moving uphill at speed), red prayer-gates and toppled fox statues providing half cover, drifting mist limiting vision beyond 30 feet, and a sheer drop on the path's outer edge (a shove or failed DC 12 Dexterity save means a 15-foot fall, 1d6 damage).

scenes.roleplayNotes: These bandits are desperate, not irredeemable — a chance for a merciful party to gain allies or information rather than just corpses. The captain knows the upper mountain has grown deadly and has heard the nue's three-voiced cry; he'll trade that knowledge for his life. A party that spares him may find the surviving ronin guarding the path on their descent, a small repayment of mercy. Honor the dice in this fight — the ronin are competent, and a careless party can be hurt. The scarred stag, if befriended, snorts a warning one round before the ambush springs, granting the party advantage on initiative.
loot: From the fallen or surrendered ronin: 2 fine katana (worth 25 gp each), a purse of mixed coin (40 gp total), and a half-eaten ration of travel food
The bandit captain's lacquered sake gourd, still half full — the sake disrupts onibi-fire if splashed (3 uses)

scenes.name: The Feral Deer-Spirits and the Hidden Clue
scenes.description: Higher on the path, where the mist thickens and the cold deepens, the party encounters what has become of the deer that strayed too near the kami's wrath: a pack of corrupted shika-spirits, their gentle nature burned away, their eyes white and weeping, charging anything that moves. Nearby, hidden in a hollow beneath a toppled fox statue, lies a clue left by the frightened young monk Ren before he fled — the key to the thief's identity and motive.
scenes.readAloud: "The mist grows thick as milk and cold as a tomb, and the prayer-gates here lean broken and lichen-eaten. Somewhere ahead, hooves strike stone — many hooves, fast and wrong. They come out of the white: deer, but not as you have seen them. Their hides are slick with the same oily red brand the scarred stag bears, their eyes rolled white and weeping black, their gentle heads lowered now to gore rather than to bow. 🦌 There is no fear in them, and no mercy — only the kami's borrowed fury, driving them down the mountain to drive you back. The scarred stag at your side lets out a low, mournful cry, as if it knows each one by name."

skillChecks.success: Holding your ground and projecting calm — or letting the scarred stag call to its lost herd-mates — you turn aside two of the corrupted deer-spirits, who break off and flee into the mist rather than fight.
skillChecks.failure: The corruption is too deep; the deer-spirits cannot be reached and charge as one.

skillChecks.success: You keep the party on the true sacred path through the disorienting mist, avoiding the sheer drops where a panicked retreat would be deadly, and you spot the disturbed earth beneath a toppled fox statue.
skillChecks.failure: The mist turns you around; you lose ground and must fight the deer-spirits on worse footing (they gain advantage on their first charge).

skillChecks.success: Beneath the toppled fox statue you find a hollow where a frightened hand hid a folded paper — a temple guard's pass bearing the name Sato, wrapped around a child's drawing and a note: 'Forgive me. She is dying. The Mirror is said to heal. I will return it. I swear it.' The thief was a desperate father.
skillChecks.failure: You find only the empty hollow, the clue overlooked in the chaos of the fight.

enemies: 4 corrupted shika-spirits (use wolf stats, reflavored as feral deer with goring antlers)
1 great corrupted stag (use dire wolf stats, reflavored)
combatEncounters.tactics: The corrupted deer use Pack Tactics, charging from the mist to gain advantage and trying to knock targets prone (DC 11 Strength save on a hit) then trampling them on the ground. The great corrupted stag leads, targeting the party's spellcasters. They feel no fear and never flee unless turned by Animal Handling. The scarred stag companion, if present, intercepts the great stag, dueling it antler-to-antler and freeing the party to handle the lesser deer — a dramatic beat where the redeemed deer fights its corrupted kin.
combatEncounters.terrain: A mist-choked switchback (vision limited to 30 feet, ranged attacks beyond that at disadvantage), broken prayer-gates and a toppled fox statue as cover and clue-cache, slick stone underfoot (DC 10 Acrobatics or fall prone when dashing), and a sheer mountain drop on the outer edge.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This fight should feel tragic — these were gentle messenger-deer twisted into weapons by a god's grief. Killing them is mercy, not victory; describe their brands cooling and their white eyes clearing in death, the corruption releasing. A party that turns some aside with Animal Handling rather than slaughtering them all should feel the moral weight of that choice. The Sato clue is the emotional hinge of the whole adventure: the thief is not a villain but a father trying to save his dying daughter, and the players should carry that knowledge into the climax. End the scene with the mist thinning above and the silhouette of the ancient cedar shrine visible at the path's top — and an unnatural, three-throated cry rolling down from the grove beyond it.
loot: Sato's temple guard pass, his daughter's drawing, and his written confession (quest items — reveal the thief's identity and tragic motive)
A vial of clear mountain spring-water from the sacred path, which counts as holy water against yokai (2 doses)

acts.title: Act 3: The Mirror and the Mountain God
acts.description: The party reaches the kami's hidden shrine on the shoulder of Mount Mikasa, recovers the stolen Mikasa Mirror from where the doomed thief abandoned it, and faces the heart of the crisis. They may choose the careful path — purify, perform the rite of appeasement exactly, restore the Mirror, and calm the god without bloodshed — or, if the rite fails or they move too aggressively, they must fight the nue, the chimera-yokai born of the kami's wounded fury. This act is the climax: a true choice between ritual and violence, with the fate of Kasuga and the deer in the balance.
objectives: Reach the hidden shrine of the Mikasa kami in the sacred grove
Find the thief Sato's body and recover the Mikasa Mirror
Perform the Ritual of Appeasement correctly to calm the kami — or fail and face its wrath
Defeat or pacify the nue, the chimera-yokai of the god's fury
Restore the Mirror to its reliquary and return to Kasuga

scenes.name: The Sacred Grove and the Thief's End
scenes.description: Above the mist, the party emerges into the clearing of the kami's mountain shrine — an unpainted cedar structure ringed by a sacred rope, standing in a stillness so deep it presses on the ears. Here they find the body of Sato, the thief, half-claimed by the corruption he loosed, the Mikasa Mirror fallen from his dead hand. And here the wronged kami's grief is thickest, on the very edge of taking monstrous shape.
scenes.readAloud: "The mist parts like a curtain and the world goes silent. You stand at the edge of a clearing where the air itself seems to hold its breath. An ancient shrine of silver-weathered cedar stands ringed by a thick sacred rope hung with white paper streamers that do not stir, though wind moves the trees beyond. ⛩️ No bird sings. No deer treads here. And before the shrine lies a man — a temple guard by his robes, fallen on his face, one outflung hand reaching for a round bronze mirror that has rolled just beyond his fingers. The oily red brand has crawled up his arm and into his hair. He is days dead, and yet his reaching hand still trembles, as if the grief that killed him will not let him rest. Above and beyond the shrine, in the dark of the sacred grove, something stirs — and cries out with three voices at once. 💀"

skillChecks.success: You understand the grove's terrible stillness: the kami's covenant with the valley is broken, and its grief hangs at the brink of becoming wrath made flesh. Restoring the Mirror and performing the rite is the only true remedy — and it must be done with perfect respect.
skillChecks.failure: The wrongness of the place is overwhelming, but you cannot tell whether ritual or steel is the answer.

skillChecks.success: Examining Sato, you confirm he died not of violence but of the corruption itself, which consumed him when the kami's grief overwhelmed the Mirror he carried. The drawing and note clutched to his chest confirm he meant only to heal his daughter.
skillChecks.failure: You see only a dead man marked by the same brand as the deer.

skillChecks.success: The Mikasa Mirror lies unbroken in the moss — a disk of ancient polished bronze, its back cast with deer and lantern motifs. Lifting it reverently (with a bow, in cloth, never by your bare reflection-facing hand) avoids stirring the kami further.
skillChecks.failure: You retrieve the Mirror, but a careless grip flares the brand-corruption, alerting the nue and forfeiting any surprise.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the moral and emotional peak of the adventure. Let the discovery of Sato land — a father who stole a god's treasure on a rumor it might cure his dying child, and who died for it on the cold mountain. Players who read his note and drawing should feel the tragedy. Make clear, through the kami's near-breaking grief and the nue's gathering cry, that they now stand at a genuine fork: the careful rite of appeasement (next scene), or the fight (the scene after). Recovering the Mirror is essential to both paths — without it, the kami cannot be calmed and the nue cannot be truly laid to rest. The scarred stag, if present, kneels at the grove's edge and will not enter, bowing its head toward the shrine for the first time in the whole adventure.
loot: The Mikasa Mirror (sacred relic, quest item — must be restored to calm the kami; a polished bronze disk cast with deer and lanterns)
Sato's last effects: his daughter's drawing, his written confession, and a small vial of fever-medicine he never delivered

scenes.name: The Ritual of Appeasement
scenes.description: Before the cedar shrine, the party may attempt the rite Hideo and Tsubaki taught them — to purify, approach with perfect etiquette, restore the Mirror, and offer the lucky go-en coin to mend the broken connection between valley and god. Done correctly, the kami's grief is soothed and its wrath dissolves before it can become a monster. Done wrong, the offended god's fury crystallizes into the nue, and the party must fight. This is an etiquette challenge with mechanically meaningful steps and pre-declared DCs.
scenes.readAloud: "You step toward the ancient shrine, the Mirror cool and heavy in your hands, the three-voiced cry rolling closer through the trees. Everything you were taught comes back to you now: the water-trough beside the shrine for purification; the deep, deliberate bows; the offering that mends a broken bond. The kami is listening — you can feel its grief like a held breath at the back of your neck — and it is weighing you. One misstep, one careless gesture, and that grief will turn to fury. But done rightly... done rightly, a god might be consoled. 🙏⛩️"

skillChecks.success: STEP 1 — Purification. You cleanse hands and mouth at the water-trough in the proper manner before approaching the sacred ground. The brand-corruption recedes a pace from the clearing's edge.
skillChecks.failure: You approach the shrine unpurified. The kami takes offense; the nue's cry sharpens. (Each failed step builds toward the fight: 2 failures and the ritual collapses into combat.)

skillChecks.success: STEP 2 — The Approach. Bow twice, clap twice, bow once, with measured reverence. Your respect is plain and the held breath of the grove eases.
skillChecks.failure: Your bows are hurried or your claps mistimed. The god's grief curdles toward anger; the brand creeps closer.

skillChecks.success: STEP 3 — Restoring the Mirror. With steady, reverent hands you set the Mikasa Mirror upon the shrine's altar-stone, never letting your own reflection meet the sacred surface, never letting it touch the ground. The Mirror settles as if it had never left.
skillChecks.failure: You fumble the placement, or your reflection flashes in the bronze. The kami recoils; the grove darkens.

skillChecks.success: STEP 4 — The Offering and the Plea. You toss the lucky go-en coin into the offering-box and speak, plainly and truly, of Sato — a grieving father, not a thief — and beg the god's mercy for the valley below. The kami hears. The corruption drains away like water into earth; the brand fades; somewhere far below, the oldest lantern of the shrine blazes alight of its own accord, and every deer in Kasuga, at last, bows its head.
skillChecks.failure: Your plea rings hollow or your offering is graceless. The god's grief breaks its banks at last — and the nue takes shape.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Run this as a four-step etiquette challenge in order. Track failures: if the party fails two or more of the four steps, the ritual collapses and the nue manifests (proceed to the next scene). If they pass at least three of four — and crucially the final Persuasion plea — the kami is appeased and no fight is needed; the adventure resolves peacefully and triumphantly here. Honor the DCs and the dice strictly: do not fudge a failed step into success, and do not deny a party their earned peaceful ending. Reward players who invoke Sato's note, who bow, who use the go-en coin Obaba Yuki gave them, who remember the exact order Tsubaki taught — let good roleplay grant advantage on these checks. Whether they win by ritual or are forced to the fight, the recovered Mirror and the truth of Sato make this a tragedy resolved, not a monster slain for loot.
loot: If the ritual succeeds: the kami's blessing — each party member gains the Blessing of Kasuga (once per long rest, reroll one failed save against fear or charm), and the deer of Kasuga bow to them ever after

scenes.name: The Nue Descends
scenes.description: If the ritual fails — or if the party chose steel over reverence — the kami's wounded fury tears itself loose from the grove and takes monstrous shape: the nue, a chimera-yokai with the face of a monkey, the body of a tiger, the legs of a great cat, and a serpent for a tail, crying with three throats at once. The party must fight it amid the sacred grove, with the recovered Mirror as the key to ending the corruption even after the beast falls.
scenes.readAloud: "The grief breaks. From the dark of the sacred grove the kami's fury pours forth and knots itself into a body — a thing of nightmare cobbled from many beasts. It has the leering face of a monkey, the striped and muscled body of a great tiger, the clawed legs of a hunting cat, and for a tail a living serpent that hisses and snaps of its own will. From its three throats comes a cry that is three cries at once — a monkey's shriek, a tiger's roar, a serpent's hiss — and the oily red brand blazes across its every limb. 💀 This is the nue: a god's wound given teeth. It fixes all three of its voices upon you and springs."

skillChecks.success: Even mid-battle you perceive that the nue is not a true monster but the kami's pain wearing a beast's shape — it cannot be permanently destroyed by force alone. Restoring the Mirror to the shrine's altar mid-fight (an action requiring a successful Religion check, DC 13) will drain its strength, halving its remaining HP and ending its corruption when it falls.
skillChecks.failure: The beast seems an ordinary, if terrible, monster to be cut down by main force.

skillChecks.success: You wrestle free of the nue's grapple or its serpent-tail's coils, avoiding being dragged into the corrupted heart of the grove.
skillChecks.failure: The serpent-tail constricts; you are restrained until you break free (DC 13 Athletics or Acrobatics).

enemies: 1 nue (chimera-yokai — use saber-toothed tiger stats as the base, with an owlbear's hit points, plus a serpent-tail attack: +5 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing and DC 13 Constitution save or be poisoned for 1 round)
combatEncounters.tactics: The nue opens with its three-voiced cry (all creatures within 30 feet make a DC 13 Wisdom save or be frightened for 1 round). It pounces with tiger's claws to knock targets prone, then uses its serpent-tail to attack and restrain a different foe each round, dragging the restrained toward the corrupted grove. It focuses the party member carrying the Mikasa Mirror, sensing the threat the relic poses. If a character succeeds in restoring the Mirror to the altar (DC 13 Religion as an action while adjacent to the altar), the nue's brand flickers and dims — halve its remaining HP, and when it next drops to 0 it dies for good rather than reforming. If the Mirror is NOT restored, the nue reforms with half HP 1d4 rounds after being reduced to 0, until the Mirror is placed. Honor the dice and the HP totals strictly — there is no phantom HP and no rigged outcome; if the party falls, that is a true and respected end.
combatEncounters.terrain: The sacred grove clearing (60 feet across) ringed by the shimenawa rope, with the cedar shrine and its altar-stone at the rear (reaching it to restore the Mirror is the fight's tactical objective), scattered cedar trunks providing cover, and the unnatural stillness broken only by the nue's three voices. The water-trough at the shrine's side holds purifying water that deals an extra 1d6 radiant damage to the nue if its water is thrown or the beast is shoved into it (DC 13 contested).

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the climactic fight, and it is winnable but genuinely dangerous — run it honestly. The key tactical and thematic beat is the Mirror: brute force alone makes the nue effectively unkillable (it reforms), but restoring the relic to the altar mid-combat breaks the corruption and lets the party end it for good. A clever party splits effort — some holding the nue while one races the Mirror to the altar. When the nue finally falls with the Mirror restored, do not narrate a generic monster-death: describe the chimera-shape dissolving into a sigh of released grief, the brand-corruption draining from the whole mountain at once, and the kami's presence settling at last into peace. Below, the oldest shrine lantern blazes alight on its own, and every deer in Kasuga bows. If the party is at risk of a TPK, the options are retreat down the path or a desperate dash to restore the Mirror — but do not invent a rescue. The dice are the dice.
loot: From the dissolved nue: a single shed serpent-scale that never tarnishes (a focus worth 50 gp, prized by spellcasters), and the lifting of the corruption from every branded deer in the valley
The Mikasa Mirror, restored to its altar (which must be returned to the Daibutsu reliquary in Kasuga to complete the quest)

scenes.name: The Deer Bow Again
scenes.description: With the kami appeased — by rite or by the nue's defeat and the Mirror's restoration — the corruption lifts from the valley. The party returns to Kasuga to restore the Mirror to its proper reliquary, report to the grateful priests, and witness the deer bow once more. This is the denouement, where the players' choices and mercies are weighed and rewarded.
scenes.readAloud: "As the last of the corruption drains from the mountain, a great stillness gives way to a greater peace. The mist burns off the cedar slopes. Far below, the oldest lantern of the shrine — dark in living memory — kindles to a steady gold all on its own, and you know the god is consoled. ⛩️🏮 When you descend at last into the deer park of Kasuga, the herd is waiting along the path, hundreds of pale heads turning toward you. And then, as one, they bow — every deer in the valley dipping its antlered head low to the earth, the way the sacred messengers of the gods have bowed for a thousand years. 🦌 The scarred stag at your side, its red brand faded clean away, bows deepest of all."

skillChecks.success: You restore the Mikasa Mirror to its reliquary behind the Daibutsu's lotus dais with the proper rites, completing the covenant's mending. The bronze Buddha's verdigris 'tears' are gone, and the hall is at peace.
skillChecks.failure: The priests must guide you through the final rite of enshrinement, but the Mirror is restored all the same.

skillChecks.success: You tell Hideo and Tsubaki the truth of Sato — that the thief was a grieving father, not a villain — and persuade the temple to see his daughter cared for and his memory shown mercy rather than scorn. The priests honor your compassion.
skillChecks.failure: The temple recovers its treasure, but Sato's name is remembered only as a thief's, and his orphaned daughter goes unaided unless the party intervenes directly.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Let the players decide how Sato's tragedy is remembered — whether his orphaned, fevered daughter (still alive, if the party hurries his undelivered fever-medicine to her) is cared for, and whether the temple grieves him or condemns him. There is no wrong answer, but the consequences differ in tone. Kannushi Hideo bows to the party as equals; Tsubaki's visions cease; Obaba Yuki weeps with relief and presses fresh crackers on them so they may feel the deer bow for themselves. If the party showed mercy to the ronin, the surviving bandits salute them on the road out. Close on the image of the bowing deer and the lit oldest-lantern — beauty restored, but earned through a genuine reckoning with grief.
loot: The temple's reward: 120 gp from the shrine's coffers and honored lodging in Kasuga whenever the party returns
If the party delivers Sato's fever-medicine to his daughter in time, she recovers — and years later may become an ally; the grateful temple gifts a potion of greater healing
Kannushi Hideo gifts a blessed deer-crest token granting safe passage and welcome at any shrine of the Floating World

culturalCodex.topic: The Bowing Deer and Deer Crackers (Shika-Senbei)
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: In Nara Park, Japan, over a thousand wild sika deer roam freely and are considered messengers of the gods. Many have genuinely learned to bow their heads to beg for shika-senbei — flat rice-and-bran crackers sold by licensed vendors for about 200 yen a stack. The deer can be pushy: once they know you have food they will nudge, nibble clothing, and headbutt, so keep crackers hidden until you're ready, feed quickly, then show your open empty hands so they know it's gone.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In Kasuga, the deer bow because a god once rode one down from the mountain, and they stop bowing when that god is dishonored. A deer's bow is a living barometer of the kami's favor, and a deer's brand-scar marks divine corruption — none of which is true of the friendly, cracker-hungry (and very real) deer of Nara.

culturalCodex.topic: The Great Bronze Buddha (Daibutsu) at Todai-ji
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Todai-ji temple in Nara houses the Daibutsu, one of the world's largest bronze Buddha statues — about 15 meters tall and cast in the 8th century from hundreds of tons of bronze. Its hall (Daibutsu-den) is among the largest wooden buildings on Earth. A pillar inside has a hole at its base said to match the Buddha's nostril; squeezing through is believed to bring good luck (it's a tight fit best left to children and the slim).
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In the adventure the bronze Buddha weeps verdigris 'tears' and a relic-mirror is hidden behind its dais — dramatic license. The real Buddha does not weep or speak, and no Mikasa Mirror sits behind it, but the colossal scale and the lucky nostril-pillar are entirely real.

culturalCodex.topic: The Lantern Festivals at Kasuga Taisha
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Kasuga Taisha shrine in Nara is famous for roughly 3,000 lanterns — bronze ones hung beneath its eaves and stone ones lining its paths, many moss-covered and centuries old. Twice a year, during the Mantoro festivals (in early February and mid-August), the priests light all of them at once, turning the vermilion shrine into a sea of flickering gold. The shrine's striking red-orange (vermilion) paint is traditional and said to ward off evil.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The 'ten thousand lanterns' and the onibi demon-fire that lures children into the forest are heightened for the story. The real festival is a peaceful, breathtaking spectacle — no yokai included — but the massed lantern-light and the vermilion shrine are real and well worth timing a trip around.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: A few words go a long way in Japan. 'Kawaii' (ka-wai-ee) means cute — perfect for the deer and the lanterns. 'Abunai' (ah-boo-nai) means dangerous or 'look out!' — shouted as a warning. 'Oishii' (oy-shee) means delicious — for the food, not the deer crackers (those are for the deer). 'Arigatou gozaimasu' is a polite thank you, and 'sumimasen' means both 'excuse me' and 'sorry.'
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In the adventure, NPCs and read-aloud sprinkle these words for flavor, and a few invented terms (kami-names, the Mikasa Mirror) are fictional. The everyday phrases above are real and genuinely useful in Nara today.

culturalCodex.topic: How to Make an Offering at a Shrine
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: At a Shinto shrine, first purify at the water-trough (temizuya): rinse your left hand, then right, then cup water to your mouth, then let water run down the dipper's handle — never drink straight from the dipper. At the main hall, toss a coin into the offering box, then bow twice, clap twice, hold a moment of prayer, and bow once more ('ni-rei, ni-hakushu, ichi-rei'). A 5-yen coin is especially auspicious: '5 yen' is 'go-en,' a pun on 'go-en,' meaning a good connection or fateful bond.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The adventure turns this etiquette into a literal mechanical 'Ritual of Appeasement' with dice and DCs, and makes the go-en coin's luck supernaturally real. The actual customs — purify, bow twice, clap twice, bow once, offer a lucky 5-yen coin — are exactly what real worshippers do.

culturalCodex.topic: Feeding Deer Safely (and Not Near Traffic)
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Nara's deer are wild animals, not pets. Don't tease them by holding crackers high — feed promptly to avoid nips and headbutts, especially in autumn rutting season when bucks can be aggressive. Critically, do NOT feed or lure deer near roads: deer-vehicle accidents are a real hazard, and feeding them roadside trains them toward traffic. Keep plastic bags and maps tucked away too — deer have been known to eat them.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In Kasuga the danger near the 'shrine path' is an angered kami and corrupted deer-spirits. In real Nara the danger is far more mundane — pushy deer and nearby traffic — but the advice to keep food hidden and stay clear of roads is genuinely good, real-world guidance.

culturalCodex.topic: Yokai and Kami in Japanese Folklore
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: 'Kami' are the gods or sacred spirits of Shinto — of mountains, rivers, trees, and shrines — who must be honored with rites and offerings. 'Yokai' are folklore creatures and spirits, from mischievous to monstrous. The 'nue' is a real legendary chimera from Japanese myth, classically described with a monkey's face, a tanuki or tiger's body, a tiger's legs, and a snake for a tail, crying in an eerie voice. 'Onibi' are ghostly demon-fires akin to will-o'-the-wisps.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The adventure gives the nue D&D stats and ties it to a specific stolen relic and grieving thief. The folkloric nue, onibi, kami, and yokai are real parts of Japanese myth — but the Mikasa kami, the corruption-brand, and Sato's story are invented for this campaign.

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: 'Miko' are shrine maidens at Shinto shrines, traditionally dressed in a white top and bright red hakama (split skirt-trousers). Among their duties is performing 'kagura,' sacred ceremonial dances offered to entertain and honor the kami, often with bells, fans, or sprigs of sacred sakaki greenery. You can sometimes see kagura performed at festivals at major shrines.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The character Tsubaki has prophetic visions and her dance helps hold a magical crowd's calm — dramatic embellishments. Real miko and their red-and-white dress and sacred dances are an authentic, living part of Japanese shrine culture.

npcsInvolved.name: Kannushi Hideo
npcsInvolved.description: A tall, soft-spoken Shinto priest in the white and pale robes of his office, Hideo carries himself with the deliberate grace of a man who has spent his life in ritual. His face is lined with new worry, and he bows more deeply than his station requires — the bow of a man ashamed to ask outsiders to do what his vows forbid him.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Hideo must save his valley and recover the stolen Mirror, but as a priest he may neither take up arms nor ascend the wrath-cursed mountain. Asking armed strangers to tread his sacred ground and shed blood shames him deeply, and he is torn between that shame and his desperate love for Kasuga and its people. He believes in mercy and will be moved by any party that shows the same.

npcsInvolved.name: Tsubaki
npcsInvolved.description: A young senior shrine maiden (miko) in white and crimson, Tsubaki is grave and quiet beyond her years, with dark eyes that seem to look slightly past the world. Since the corruption began she has been plagued by visions of a 'three-voiced beast' descending the mountain, and she performs the sacred kagura dances with a tension that the other maidens have begun to fear.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Tsubaki is bound by duty to remain at the shrine even as her visions terrify her. She wants the party to succeed both to save the valley and to silence the dreams that have stolen her sleep. She teaches the party the rite of appeasement and the offering of the go-en coin, and her visions provide foreshadowing the party can act on if they listen.

npcsInvolved.name: Obaba Yuki
npcsInvolved.description: A tiny, sun-wrinkled old woman who has sold shika-senbei at the edge of the deer park for sixty years, Yuki knows every deer by sight and most of them by temperament. Her hands are never still, twisting her apron or breaking crackers, and her eyes miss nothing. She speaks in proverbs and old legends and is the first to insist the gods are unhappy.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Yuki loves the deer as her own children and is heartbroken that they no longer bow. She wants the old harmony restored and will help any party that treats the deer — and her — with respect, teaching them how to feed the herd properly and gifting a lucky go-en coin 'for connection.' She is the warm human heart of the deer park.

npcsInvolved.name: Sato (The Thief)
npcsInvolved.description: In life, Sato was a quiet, dutiful temple guard, devoted to his wife and small daughter. The party never meets him alive — they find his body in the sacred grove, half-claimed by the corruption, the stolen Mirror fallen from his reaching hand and his daughter's drawing clutched to his chest. The oily red brand has crept up his arm and into his hair.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Sato stole the Mikasa Mirror on a desperate rumor that its sacred power could cure his daughter, who lay dying of fever. He swore in a note to return it once she was healed. Instead, the kami's grief at the broken covenant corrupted and killed him on the mountain. He is not a villain but a grieving father, and his story is the moral heart of the adventure — a reminder that the source of all this ruin was love, not malice.

npcsInvolved.name: Ren
npcsInvolved.description: A young, earnest novice monk who carried Hideo's summoning letter to the party along the pilgrim road, Ren is brave in spirit but timid in practice. He fled the lower mountain path when the corruption began, but not before hiding a crucial clue — Sato's guard-pass and confession — beneath a toppled fox statue.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Ren wants to be of use and to atone for fleeing the mountain in fear. He can guide the party to Kasuga, vouch for them with the priests, and — if asked — confirm where he hid the clue. He looks up to the adventurers and may grow into a recurring ally across the campaign.

npcsInvolved.name: The Ronin Captain
npcsInvolved.description: A masterless swordsman fallen on hard times, the ronin captain leads a band of starving ex-warriors who have turned to robbing pilgrims on the lower mountain path. Beneath his cold menace is a man ashamed of what desperation has made him, and a flicker of the honor he once lived by.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The captain wants to survive and feed his men in a valley the gods have abandoned. He can be fought, frightened off, or appealed to through his lost honor. If spared, he trades knowledge of the 'beast that screams with many voices' and may repay mercy by guarding the party's descent — a small redemption.

rewards.gold: 175 gp total (120 gp temple reward, 40 gp from the ronin's purse, 15 gp from the rescued child's grateful family)
items: The Blessing of Kasuga (if the kami is appeased — once per long rest, reroll a failed save against fear or charm)
Shrine charms (omamori) — single-use wards against yokai fear/charm effects
Blessed deer-crest token (safe passage and welcome at any shrine of the Floating World)
A nue serpent-scale focus (worth 50 gp, prized by spellcasters)
Potion of Greater Healing (if Sato's daughter is saved with his undelivered medicine)
The Mikasa Mirror (sacred relic, restored to the temple — not kept by the party)
rewards.story: The party has mended a broken covenant between a mountain god and the sacred valley of Kasuga, lifted a corruption that twisted gentle deer into weapons, and reckoned with the truth that all this ruin sprang from a father's love rather than any villain's malice. The deer bow again, the oldest lantern of the shrine burns once more, and the priests of Kasuga count the party honored friends of the Floating World. How they remembered Sato — as thief or as grieving father — and whether they saved his orphaned daughter will echo in the valley's gratitude, and word of their deeds may reach other shrines and other kami in need.

twists: The thief was not a villain but a grieving father — Sato, a temple guard — who stole the Mikasa Mirror on a desperate rumor it could cure his dying daughter, and who was killed by the very corruption his theft unleashed. The source of all this ruin was love, not malice.

The angered kami is not evil and was never the enemy. Its grief at the broken covenant simply curdled into wrath; restore the Mirror and perform the proper rite, and the god's fury becomes a blessing and the deer bow again.

The monstrous nue is not a true monster to be slain for loot, but the kami's wounded fury given a chimera's shape — it cannot be permanently killed by force alone, only ended by restoring the sacred Mirror to its altar.

Etiquette is the real weapon. The careful Ritual of Appeasement — purify, bow twice, clap twice, bow once, offer the go-en coin — can resolve the entire climax without a single sword drawn, if the party paid attention to the customs they were taught.
dmTips: Lead with beauty, then undercut it. Every location in Kasuga should first dazzle — golden light, bowing deer, ten thousand lanterns, a colossal serene Buddha — before the wrongness shows through. The horror lands hardest against a backdrop of fragile loveliness.

Make etiquette mechanical and rewarding. Reward players who bow, who keep deer crackers hidden, who purify before approaching a shrine, who remember the offering order — grant them advantage on social and ritual checks. This teaches the customs the climax depends on, and makes cultural respect feel powerful rather than decorative.

Offer the peaceful path honestly. The Ritual of Appeasement can resolve Act 3 with no combat at all. Do not railroad the party into fighting the nue — if they earn the ritual, give them the peaceful, triumphant ending. Conversely, do not deny them the fight if they choose steel or fail the rite. Both endings are valid; the dice and their choices decide.

Honor Sato's tragedy. The clue beneath the fox statue and his body in the grove are the emotional core. Don't rush past them. Let the players read his note and his daughter's drawing, and let their treatment of his memory — and whether they save his orphaned child with his undelivered medicine — carry real weight in the denouement.

Run the nue fight straight. It is genuinely dangerous and the Mirror is the key — brute force alone makes it reform endlessly. Track HP honestly, honor natural 1s and 20s, and if the party falls, respect the outcome rather than inventing a rescue. The recovery mechanism is restoring the Mirror, not narrative hand-waving.

Use the scarred stag as a thread. If the party calms it in Act 1, weave it through every act — guiding the path, warning of ambushes, dueling its corrupted kin, kneeling at the grove, and bowing deepest of all at the end. It gives the whole adventure a beating heart.
